options.text: The rubbish was being thrown away

The correct answer is: The rubbish was thrown away

Rule: The active sentence is in Simple Past tense ('threw'). The passive formula for Simple Past is: Object + was/were + past participle (V3).

Active: We threw away the rubbish. → Passive: The rubbish was thrown away (by us).

'Threw' → past participle: 'thrown'. 'The rubbish' (singular) → 'was thrown'.

Why other options are wrong:

Option 2 — 'The rubbish thrown away': Missing the auxiliary verb 'was'; incomplete passive form.

Option 3 — 'The rubbish was being thrown away': This is Past Continuous Passive; the active is Simple Past, not Past Continuous.

Option 4 — 'The rubbish will be thrown away': Future tense; does not match the past tense original.

Correct answer: Option 1 — The rubbish was thrown away

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: died for (B)

Full sentence: 'The old man died for a heart attack today.'

The error is in segment B: 'died for' is incorrect. The correct preposition is 'of'. One dies OF a disease, illness, or cause — not 'for'.

The correct answer is: The staff was making the flight announcement when I entered.

The passive sentence uses Past Continuous Passive: 'was being made'. Converting to Active Voice:

Past Continuous Passive: was being + V3 → Active Past Continuous: was + V-ing

Passive: The flight announcement was being made by the staff when I entered.

Active: The staff was making the flight announcement when I entered.

The time clause 'when I entered' is retained as is.

Why other options are wrong:

Option 1 — 'The staff made': Simple Past; loses the ongoing/continuous aspect.

Option 2 — 'The flight announcement made the staff': Subject/object swapped; nonsensical.

Option 4 — 'The staff has made': Present Perfect; changes tense incorrectly.

Correct answer: Option 3 — The staff was making the flight announcement when I entered.

questions.question: Choose the correct option to rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph: A. The new recruit saluted with nervous energy. B. The sergeant nodded with a knowing smile. C. He remembered his own first day on duty. D. Time had taught him both discipline and patience.
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the correct option to rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:

A. The new recruit saluted with nervous energy.

B. The sergeant nodded with a knowing smile.

C. He remembered his own first day on duty.

D. Time had taught him both discipline and patience.
questions.solution:
The correct order is: A B C D

Logical sequence:

A: Introduces the scene — 'The new recruit saluted with nervous energy.' (Setting: a new soldier's nervousness)

B: Introduces the sergeant's response — 'The sergeant nodded with a knowing smile.' (The experienced officer's reaction)

C: The sergeant reflects — 'He remembered his own first day on duty.' (Connection: the sergeant was once like this recruit)

D: Conclusion/wisdom — 'Time had taught him both discipline and patience.' (What experience brought him)

The narrative flows: new recruit's nervousness → sergeant's reaction → sergeant's reflection → the lesson time taught.

Correct answer: Option 1 — A B C D

questions.question: Choose the right meaning of the idiom 'go the extra mile' in the sentence: The team went the extra mile to meet the client's needs.
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the right meaning of the idiom 'go the extra mile' in the sentence:

The team went the extra mile to meet the client's needs.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: Made additional effort

'Go the extra mile' means to make more effort than is expected or required; to put in additional work to achieve a goal. In the sentence, the team went beyond what was required to satisfy the client.

Why other options are wrong:

Option 1 — Took a long route: This is a literal interpretation; the idiom has nothing to do with physical travel routes.

Option 3 — Spent more money: The idiom refers to extra effort, not extra expenditure.

Option 4 — Traveled abroad: Completely literal and incorrect.

Correct answer: Option 2 — Made additional effort

questions.question: Select the correct meaning of the idiom 'kick the bucket' as used in the sentence below: He passed on all his belongings to his nephew before he kicked the bucket.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the correct meaning of the idiom 'kick the bucket' as used in the sentence below:

He passed on all his belongings to his nephew before he kicked the bucket.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: Died

'Kick the bucket' is an informal idiom meaning to die. In the sentence, 'He passed on all his belongings to his nephew before he kicked the bucket' — passing on belongings and then 'kicking the bucket' clearly means he died.

Why other options are wrong:

Option 1 — Went on vacation: No connection to this idiom's meaning.

Option 3 — Bought a farm: This is actually another informal idiom for death in some dialects, but in this question 'Died' is the correct answer.

Option 4 — Got angry: No connection to this idiom.

Correct answer: Option 2 — Died

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'burned the midnight oil' as used in the sentence below: Jonathan and his friends burned the midnight oil to complete their final project.
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'burned the midnight oil' as used in the sentence below:

Jonathan and his friends burned the midnight oil to complete their final project.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: Worked late at night

'Burn the midnight oil' means to stay up and work late into the night. The phrase originates from the time when people used oil lamps for light, and burning oil at midnight meant working very late.

In the sentence, Jonathan and his friends stayed up late to complete their project.

Why other options are wrong:

Option 2 — Slept well: Opposite of the idiom's meaning — burning the midnight oil means NOT sleeping.

Option 3 — Celebrated: Has nothing to do with working late.

Option 4 — Lit candles: This is the literal interpretation; the idiom is purely figurative.

Correct answer: Option 1 — Worked late at night

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'go the extra mile' in the sentence: She always goes the extra mile to support her students.

questions.solution:

'Go the extra mile' means to put in more effort or work than is expected in order to help someone or achieve something. A teacher who 'goes the extra mile' for students does more than the basic requirements to support them.

Option 1 — Travels more: Literal interpretation; the idiom is figurative.

Correct answer: Option 2 — Puts in extra effort

questions.question: Choose the correct indirect speech of the sentence: She said, "Why didn't anyone inform me about the change?"
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the correct indirect speech of the sentence:

She said, "Why didn't anyone inform me about the change?"

options.text: She asked why had no one informed her about the change.
options.html: She asked why had no one informed her about the change.

options.text: She said why was no one informing her.
options.html: She said why was no one informing her.

options.text: She asked why no one had informed her about the change.
options.html: She asked why no one had informed her about the change.

options.text: She asked why didn't anyone inform her about the change.
options.html: She asked why didn't anyone inform her about the change.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: She asked why no one had informed her about the change.

The original sentence is a 'Wh-question' in reported speech. Rules for reporting Wh-questions:

1. Reporting verb: 'said' → 'asked'.

2. The Wh-word ('Why') is retained.

3. The question structure is changed to affirmative (statement) order: Subject + Verb.

4. Tense backshift: 'didn't inform' (Simple Past negative) → 'had informed' (Past Perfect).

5. Pronoun: 'anyone' → 'no one' (to maintain the negative meaning without 'didn't').

6. Pronoun: 'me' → 'her'.

Reported: 'She asked why no one had informed her about the change.'

Why other options are wrong:

Option 1 — 'why had no one informed': Inverted (question) word order used; in indirect speech, affirmative order is needed.

Option 2 — 'She said why was no one informing': Uses 'said' instead of 'asked' and has inverted order.

Option 4 — 'why didn't anyone inform': Retains the direct question format with 'didn't'; not correct for indirect speech.

Correct answer: Option 3 — She asked why no one had informed her about the change.

questions.question: Choose the correct indirect speech of the sentence: She said, "Don't you understand the seriousness of the matter?"
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the correct indirect speech of the sentence:

She said, "Don't you understand the seriousness of the matter?"

options.text: She asked why I didn't understand the serious matter.
options.html: She asked why I didn't understand the serious matter.

options.text: She asked whether I didn't understand the seriousness of the matter.
options.html: She asked whether I didn't understand the seriousness of the matter.

options.text: She asked if I understood the seriousness of the matter.
options.html: She asked if I understood the seriousness of the matter.

options.text: She asked do I understand how serious it is.
options.html: She asked do I understand how serious it is.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: She asked if I understood the seriousness of the matter.

The original sentence is a Yes/No question ('Don't you understand...?'). Rules for reporting Yes/No questions:

1. Reporting verb: 'said' → 'asked'.

2. Introduce the reported question with 'if' or 'whether'.

3. Change to affirmative (statement) word order: Subject + Verb.

4. Tense backshift: 'understand' (present) → 'understood' (past).

5. Pronoun: 'you' → 'I'; 'the matter' stays.

Reported: 'She asked if I understood the seriousness of the matter.'

Why other options are wrong:

Option 1 — 'why I didn't understand': Uses 'why' — but the original is a Yes/No question, not a Wh-question. 'If/whether' must be used.

Option 2 — 'whether I didn't understand': While 'whether' is acceptable, using 'didn't understand' retains the negative — in indirect speech, 'Don't you...?' becomes affirmative 'if I understood...', not 'if I didn't understand'.

Option 4 — 'asked do I understand': Inverted question order retained; incorrect for indirect speech.

Correct answer: Option 3 — She asked if I understood the seriousness of the matter.

questions.question: Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence: He is more wiser than his brother.
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

He is more wiser than his brother.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: wiser than his brother

The highlighted phrase 'more wiser than' is incorrect because it uses a double comparative — both 'more' and '-er' (wiser) are comparative forms. You should use only one form, not both.

Rule: One-syllable and some two-syllable adjectives form comparatives by adding '-er': wise → wiser.

Correct: 'He is wiser than his brother.' ✓

Wrong: 'He is more wiser than...' — double comparative is grammatically incorrect.

Why other options are wrong:

Option 1 — 'very wise than': 'Very' is a degree adverb used for superlatives/positives, not comparatives. 'Wise than' without 'more' or '-er' is also incorrect.

Option 2 — 'more wise than': 'Wise' is a one-syllable adjective — it should use '-er' (wiser), not 'more'. 'More wise' is non-standard.

Option 3 — 'wiser to his brother': Incorrect preposition; comparatives use 'than', not 'to'.

Correct answer: Option 4 — wiser than his brother
